 4          •   With four exceptions, SPS’s CCOSS generally comports with accepted
 5              practice and is consistent with cost causation.

 7              transmission plant and related costs, both between regulatory jurisdictions
 8              and within the New Mexico (NM) retail jurisdiction. SPS asserts that this
 9              practice is required under the terms of the Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP)
10              Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) regulated Open Access
11              Transmission Tariff (OATT) and, as a result, SPS incurs higher SPP-
12              related transmission expenses. However, SPS is unable to quantify the
13              impact of BTMG load on these expenses. Thus, there are no specific
14              identifiable costs incurred by SPS attributable to serving BTMG load.
15              Further, this Commission is under no obligation to follow FERC’s costing
16              and pricing practices in setting retail rates.
17          •   Cost allocation should reflect the service a utility actually provides to its
18              customers. However, SPS does not actually serve BTMG load to the
19              extent that energy is generated and consumed behind the meter. Thus,
20              there is no legitimate reason to include BTMG load in allocating
21              transmission plant and related costs.
22          •   Further, there is no consensus among SPS members that BTMG load
23              should be included in allocating SPP-related expenses to network
24              customers based on the load ratio share each network customer reports.
25              However, even if it was appropriate to include BTMG load in allocating
26              SPP-related expenses, there is no requirement to include BTMG load in
27              allocating SPS’s transmission plant and related costs.
28          •   For all of these reasons, the Commission should reject SPS’s BTMG
29              adjustments to the transmission system peak demands used to allocate
30              SPS’s transmission plant, related costs, and SPP-related expenses, either
31              between regulatory jurisdictions or within the NM retail jurisdiction.

34              to allocate thermal production plant and the vast majority of transmission
35              plant and related base rate costs, which is consistent with cost causation.
36              Under AED-4CP, average demand is weighted by the system load factor,
37              and excess demand is weighted by one minus the system load factor.

                                2. CLASS COST-OF-SERVICE STUDY
 1   Background

 2   Q        WHAT IS A CLASS COST-OF-SERVICE STUDY?

 3   A        A CCOSS is an analysis used to determine each customer class’s responsibility for a

 4            utility’s costs and whether the revenues generated by each class are sufficient to cover

 5            the costs to serve those customers. In the context of a CCOSS, a class represents a

 6            group of customers with similar usage patterns and service characteristics. These

 7            studies are usually conducted in three phases. First, costs are distinguished by type

 8            in a process called functionalization. The causes of these costs are then identified in

 9            a second process called classification. Lastly, these costs are then assigned to each

10            of the customer classes based upon their responsibility for incurring each cost in a

11            process known as allocation.      The procedures typically used in a CCOSS are

12            described in greater detail in Appendix C.


13   Q        HAVE YOU IDENTIFIED ANY ISSUES IN SPS’S CLASS COST-OF-SERVICE

14            STUDY?

15   A        Yes. I have identified several issues related to SPS’s treatment of BTMG load,

16            calculation and application of the AED-4CP allocators, allocation of regional market

17            expense, allocation of uncollectible expense, and treatment of the LGS-T class.

21                    A generation unit that is connected on the load side of a load Meter
22                    Settlement Location and is used by the load Market Participant that is
23                    the registered owner for the Meter Settlement Location to serve all or
24                    part of its capacity, Energy or Ancillary Service needs.1

 1   Q         WHAT IS THE AED-4CP METHOD?

 2   A         AED-4CP is a variation of the Average and Excess method. Average and Excess is

 3             one of several methodologies recognized in the National Association of Regulatory

 4             Utility Commissioners’ Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manual (NARUC CAM) that

 5             explicitly considers energy usage in developing allocation factors. The AED-4CP

 6             allocation factors are derived as follows:

 7                              AED = (AD% x SLF%) + [ED% x (1-SLF%)]

 8                    Where:
 9                    AD% = A class’s share of Average Demand (or energy usage);
10                    ED% = A class’s share of Excess Demand, which is the difference
11                          between a class’s Peak Demand and its Average Demand; and
12                    SLF% = System Load Factor.6

13                    The AD component of AED is the product of each class’s percent of average

14             demand (i.e., energy consumption) and the system load factor. This measures the

15             amount of capacity costs that would be incurred if the utility served the same size load

16             at a constant 100% load factor.7

17                    The ED component of AED measures the relative variability of each class’s

18             load. The greater a class’s load variability, the greater the amount of load-following

19             resources (e.g., simple-cycle and combined-cycle gas turbines) needed to provide

20             service.

21                    Under AED-4CP, ED is the higher of (1) the difference between a class’s 4CP

22             demand and its corresponding AD or (2) zero. Thus, a class operating at a 100% load

 2             Thus, AED-4CP recognizes two important cost drivers:

 3                 • Off-peak loads do not contribute to a utility’s capacity needs to the same
 4                   degree as comparable on-peak loads; and
 5                 • Very high load factor loads are relatively flat, and for this reason they have
 6                   much less variability than do low load factor loads.

 7             Load Factor Weighting

 8   Q         WHAT LOAD FACTOR IS SPS USING IN ITS APPLICATION OF THE AED-4CP

 9             METHOD IN THIS CASE?

10   A         SPS is appropriately using its system-wide, rather than the NM retail, load factor.

11             However, SPS is using 4CP to measure system load factor.8 This is not a proper

12             definition of system load factor.


13   Q         WHAT IS 4CP?

14   A         4CP is the average of the four system peak demands during the summer months (June

15             through September).


16   Q         WHAT IS SYSTEM LOAD?

 1   Q         WHAT IS CLASS REVENUE ALLOCATION?

 2   A         Class revenue allocation refers to the assignment of a revenue change among a

 3             utility’s customer classes. The process is ideally and typically informed by the results

 4             of a CCOSS, but utilities often use some degree of judgment in assigning the base

 5             revenue increase to various customer classes, which can cause deviation from cost-

 8             PROCEEDING BE SPREAD AMONG THE CUSTOMER CLASSES?

10             class as closely as practicable. However, regulators may consider the concept of

11             gradualism to prevent customer classes from experiencing an excessively large rate

12             increase over a short time span. Under gradualism, the movement to cost-based rates

13             is made materially — but gradually — over a period of time, rather than all at once.

 7   Q         SHOULD SPS NEED AN INCENTIVE TO OPTIMIZE ITS PARTICIPATION IN THE

 9   A         No. SPP dispatches all resources within the SPP market based upon data and

10             information provided by market participants. A generation owner, such as SPS, sells

11             all of the energy from its generating resources that are dispatched by SPP. Then SPS,

12             also in its separate capacity as a load serving entity, purchases all of the energy

13             necessary to serve its customers’ load. Thus, off-system sales are, by definition, the

14             result of netting the amount of generation a utility sells into the SPP market and the

15             amount of native load that it serves by purchasing power from the SPP market. This

16             netting process provides SPS an opportunity to monetize the value of its generating

17             resources by maximizing unit availability and minimizing operating costs — actions

18             that a prudent utility undertakes in the normal course of business which are consistent

19             with its obligation to serve. Consequently, no extra effort or resources are required

20             from SPS to engage in off-system sales — they are effectively predetermined by SPP.

         PROCEDURE FOR CONDUCTING A CLASS COST-OF-SERVICE STUDY


 1   Q    WHAT PROCEDURES ARE USED IN A COST-OF-SERVICE STUDY?

 2   A    The basic procedure for conducting a CCOSS is fairly simple. First, we identify the

 3        different types of costs (functionalization), determine their primary causative factors

 4        (classification), and then apportion each item of cost among the various rate classes

 5        (allocation). Adding up the individual pieces gives the total cost for each class.

 6               Identifying the utility’s different levels of operation is a process referred to as

 7        functionalization.   The utility’s investments and expenses are separated into

 8        production, transmission, distribution, and other functions. To a large extent, this is

 9        done in accordance with the Uniform System of Accounts developed by FERC.

10               Once costs have been functionalized, the next step is to identify the primary

11        causative factor (or factors). This step is referred to as classification. Costs are

12        classified as demand-related, energy-related or customer-related.           Demand (or

13        capacity) related costs vary with peak demand, which is measured in kilowatts (kW).

14        This includes production, transmission, and some distribution investment and related

15        fixed Operation and Maintenance (O&M) expenses. As explained later, peak demand

16        determines the amount of capacity needed for reliable service. Energy-related costs

17        vary with the production of energy, which is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh).

18        Energy-related costs include fuel and variable O&M expense. Customer-related costs

19        vary directly with the number of customers and include expenses such as meters,

20        service drops, billing, and customer service.

 6   Q   WHAT KEY PRINCIPLES ARE RECOGNIZED IN A CLASS COST-OF-SERVICE

 7       STUDY?

 8   A   A properly conducted CCOSS recognizes two key cost-causation principles. First,

 9       customers are served at different delivery voltages.        This affects the amount of

10       investment the utility must make to deliver electricity to the meter. Second, since

11       cost-causation is also related to how electricity is used, both the timing and rate of

12       energy consumption (i.e., demand) are critical. Because electricity cannot be stored

13       for any significant time period, a utility must acquire sufficient generation resources

14       and construct the required transmission facilities to meet the maximum projected

15       demand, including a reserve margin as a contingency against forced and unforced

16       outages, severe weather, and load forecast error. Customers that use electricity

17       during the critical peak hours cause the utility to invest in generation and transmission

18       facilities.

 3   industrial consumers are less costly to serve on a per-unit basis because they:

 4      •   operate at higher load factors;
 5      •   take service at higher delivery voltages; and

 7   Further, non-firm service is a lower quality of service than firm service. Thus, non-firm

11          For example, the difference in the losses incurred to deliver electricity at the

12   various delivery voltages is a reason why the per-unit energy cost to serve is not the

13   same for all customers. More losses occur to deliver electricity at distribution voltage

14   (either primary or secondary) than at transmission voltage, which is generally the level

15   at which industrial customers take service. This means that the cost per kWh is lower

16   for a transmission customer than a distribution customer. The cost to deliver a kWh

17   at primary distribution, though higher than the per-unit cost at transmission, is lower

18   than the delivered cost at secondary distribution.

19          In addition to lower losses, transmission customers do not use the distribution

20   system. Instead, transmission customers construct and own their own distribution

21   systems.   Thus, distribution system costs are not allocated to transmission level

22   customers who do not use that system. Distribution customers, by contrast, require

23   substantial investments in these lower voltage facilities to provide service. Secondary

 3          Two other cost drivers are efficiency and size. These drivers are important

 5          Efficiency can be measured in terms of load factor. Load factor is the ratio of

 6   average demand (i.e., energy usage divided by the number of hours in the period) to

 7   peak demand. A customer that operates at a high load factor is more efficient than a

“NET” VS “GROSS” LOAD REPORTING

 • Load as metered at a delivery point is “net of“ (i.e., reduced
   by) the output of any generation behind (i.e., on the load side
   of) the meter at the delivery point.
 • Thus, to determine the “gross” Network Load at a delivery
   point, the output of any behind-the-meter generation would
   need to be added to metered load at that delivery point.
  • Stated another way, metered load at the delivery point must
    be grossed up by the output of the behind-the-meter
    generation to determine the delivery point’s Network Load.
